# Pauli errors and exact correction

Ignoring global phase, an $n$-qubit Pauli operator can be represented by a binary symplectic vector

$$
P(x,z)=X^xZ^z,
\qquad (x,z)\in\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}.
$$

Two Paulis commute exactly when their symplectic inner product vanishes:

$$
\langle(x,z),(x',z')\rangle_s=x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'=0.
$$

::: {#thm-qec-knill-laflamme .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: Knill--Laflamme condition

Let $P_C$ project onto a code space $C$, and let $\{E_a\}$ be a set of errors. The errors are simultaneously correctable if and only if there are scalars $\alpha_{ab}$ such that

$$
P_CE_a^\dagger E_bP_C=\alpha_{ab}P_C
$$

for every $a,b$ [@knill1997theory].
:::

This condition says that the environment may learn which error occurred, but it must not learn anything about the encoded state.

# Stabilizer codes

::: {#def-qec-stabilizer-code .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: stabilizer code

An $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code is the joint $+1$ eigenspace of an abelian subgroup $\mathcal S$ of the $n$-qubit Pauli group, with $-I\notin\mathcal S$. If $\mathcal S$ has $n-k$ independent generators, then the code space has dimension $2^k$.
:::

The normalizer $\mathcal N(\mathcal S)$ contains Paulis that preserve the code space. Logical Pauli operators are equivalence classes in $\mathcal N(\mathcal S)/\mathcal S$. The distance is

$$
d=\min\{\operatorname{wt}(P):P\in\mathcal N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S\}.
$$

This algebraic description turns error correction into a sequence of commuting parity measurements [@gottesman1997stabilizer].

## Syndrome map

Choose stabilizer generators $S_1,\ldots,S_m$. The syndrome of a Pauli $E$ is $s(E)\in\mathbb{F}_2^m$, where

$$
s_i(E)=
\begin{cases}
0,& ES_i=S_iE,\\
1,& ES_i=-S_iE.
\end{cases}
$$

If two errors have the same syndrome, then $E^\dagger F\in\mathcal N(\mathcal S)$. They are logically equivalent only when $E^\dagger F\in\mathcal S$.

::: {#def-qec-degeneracy .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: degeneracy

Two physical errors $E$ and $F$ are **degenerate with respect to the code** when they have the same action on the code space, equivalently $E^\dagger F\in\mathcal S$ up to phase.
:::

Degeneracy is therefore finer than syndrome equivalence: equal syndromes may differ either by a stabilizer or by a nontrivial logical operator.

# CSS codes

Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes separate $X$- and $Z$-type checks [@calderbank1996good; @steane1996error]. Let

$$
H_X\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m_X\times n},
\qquad
H_Z\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m_Z\times n}.
$$

Rows of $H_X$ specify $X$ stabilizers and rows of $H_Z$ specify $Z$ stabilizers. Commutativity is equivalent to

$$
H_XH_Z^{\mathsf T}=0.
$$

The number of logical qubits is

$$
k=n-\operatorname{rank}H_X-\operatorname{rank}H_Z.
$$

For independent $X$ and $Z$ noise, the two components can be decoded separately through binary syndrome equations. Under depolarizing or correlated noise, separate decoding discards $X$--$Z$ correlations and is generally suboptimal.

![A distance-three rotated surface-code patch and representative syndrome-extraction circuits.](../figures/rotated-surface-code-distance-3.jpg){#fig-qec-rotated-surface-code fig-alt="A distance-three rotated surface code with X and Z checks and two ancilla measurement circuits."}

# Chain complexes and CSS codes

Many CSS constructions arise from a length-two chain complex

$$
C_2\xrightarrow{\partial_2}C_1\xrightarrow{\partial_1}C_0,
\qquad \partial_1\partial_2=0.
$$

After choosing bases, take

$$
H_X=\partial_1,
\qquad
H_Z=\partial_2^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Then $H_XH_Z^{\mathsf T}=\partial_1\partial_2=0$. Logical $Z$ operators are homology classes

$$
H_1=\ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2,
$$

and logical $X$ operators are the corresponding cohomology classes. This language underlies [homological and hyperbolic surface codes](../construction/homological-and-hyperbolic-codes.qmd).

# What should a quantum decoder optimize?

Fix a measured syndrome $s$ and one compatible Pauli $E_s$. Every compatible error belongs to one of the logical cosets

$$
E_sL\mathcal S,
\qquad L\in\mathcal N(\mathcal S)/\mathcal S.
$$

::: {#def-qec-decoders .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: physical MAP and logical ML

A **physical-error MAP decoder** selects

$$
\widehat E_{\mathrm{MAP}}
\in\arg\max_{E:s(E)=s}\Pr(E).
$$

A **degenerate maximum-likelihood decoder** selects the logical coset

$$
\widehat L_{\mathrm{ML}}
\in\arg\max_L
\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}\Pr(E_sLS).
$$
:::

The second objective is operationally correct: recovery succeeds whenever the actual error and chosen correction differ by a stabilizer. A minimum-weight or max-product decoder instead chooses one representative. It can be suboptimal when a slightly less probable representative belongs to a much more probable coset because that coset contains many likely errors.

# Noise models and success criteria

Decoder claims are meaningful only together with a noise model and a success criterion.

- **Code-capacity noise:** data errors occur, and syndrome measurements are perfect.
- **Phenomenological noise:** data and syndrome-bit errors occur over repeated rounds.
- **Circuit-level noise:** faults occur at preparations, gates, idling locations, and measurements.

For a proposed correction $C(s)$ and actual error $E$, syndrome consistency checks whether $s(C)=s(E)$. Logical success is stronger:

$$
C(s)E\in\mathcal S.
$$

The threshold is a property of a code family, decoder, noise model, and syndrome-extraction schedule—not of the code alone [@dennis2002topological].
